w: Built as a Baroque summer retreat between 1699 and 1735, this hilltop palace looked out over its own Baroque garden -- now Frederiksberg Gardens, next door to the zoo. The royals moved out by the mid-1800s; since 1869 the halls have echoed with cadets, home to the Royal Danish Military Academy.
s: Royal summer palace, now a military academy
_facts: Baroque residence built 1699-1735
royal summer residence until mid-19th century
adjacent to Copenhagen Zoo, overlooks Frederiksberg Gardens
houses the Royal Danish Military Academy since 1869

w: Squatted from an abandoned army barracks in 1971, this self-declared 'freetown' became Europe's most famous anarchist commune -- its own flag, its own rules, and for decades an open-air hash market on Pusher Street. In 2024 residents and police finally dug the street up together, ending the trade.
_facts: began 1971 as a squatted military base in Christianshavn
intentional community, anarchist commune and micronation
Pusher Street was famous for open illegal cannabis trade until 2024
street physically dug up in a joint police/resident effort

w: Opened in 1843, this pleasure garden is the world's second-oldest amusement park still running, beaten only by another Danish park up the coast. With 4.25 million visitors in 2024 it remains Scandinavia's most-visited attraction, its fairy lights and flowerbeds sitting right next to the central station.
s: 1843 pleasure garden, still Scandinavia's biggest draw
_facts: opened 15 August 1843
second-oldest operating amusement park in the world after Dyrehavsbakken
4.25 million visitors in 2024, most-visited amusement park in Scandinavia
located downtown next to Central rail station

w: Christian IV commissioned this as a country summerhouse in 1606, then kept building until 1624 turned it into a full Dutch Renaissance castle -- typical of the king's relentless building projects. Architects Bertel Lange and Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger carried the expansion through to its final form.
_facts: built as a country summerhouse from 1606
Dutch Renaissance style, one of Christian IV's many architectural projects
expanded several times to reach final form by 1624
architects: Bertel Lange and Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger

w: Christian IV's 17th-century stock exchange is instantly recognisable for the four dragon tails twisted into a 56-metre spire above its roofline. It stood on Slotsholmen for over 380 years -- until a fire tore through the building on 16 April 2024 and toppled the dragon spire itself.
s: Dragon-tail spire, toppled by a 2024 fire
_facts: 17th-century commodity bourse and stock exchange, built 1619-1640 under Christian IV
on Slotsholmen next to Christiansborg Palace
spire shaped as four twined dragon tails, 56m tall
severely damaged by fire on 16 April 2024, which toppled the spire

w: Denmark's largest museum of cultural history sits just off Strøget, spanning archaeology, ethnology, numismatics and natural science, with exhibits pulled in from Greenland to South America. It's also the legal keeper of Danefæ, the treasure Danish law requires anyone who finds it to hand over to the Crown.
_facts: Denmark's largest museum of cultural history
short distance from Strøget at the centre of Copenhagen
exhibits from around the world, Greenland to South America
handles Danefæ, the National Treasures Danish law requires be surrendered

w: Denmark's national gallery holds the country's own collection of art, spanning Danish and foreign works from the 14th century right up to the present day, gathered, registered and researched under one roof in the centre of the city. Everyone just calls it SMK.
s: Denmark's national art gallery, SMK for short
_facts: Danish national gallery, located in central Copenhagen
collects Danish and foreign art from the 14th century to the present

w: Denmark's national opera house cost roughly 2.5 billion kroner to build -- about 370 million dollars -- making it one of the most expensive opera houses ever constructed anywhere in the world. It rises on the island of Holmen, across the harbour from the old city it faces.
s: One of the world's priciest opera houses
_facts: national opera house of Denmark
cost about 2.5 billion DKK (c. 370 million USD), among the most expensive opera houses ever built
located on the island of Holmen in central Copenhagen

w: This 17th-century canal runs from Kongens Nytorv down to the harbour, its quay lined with candy-coloured townhouses that have barely changed since the 1700s. Old wooden ships still moor along the water, and the bars and cafes behind them have been drawing a crowd for three centuries.
_facts: 17th-century waterfront and canal, stretching from Kongens Nytorv to the Inner Harbour
lined by brightly coloured 17th and early 18th century townhouses
many historical wooden ships still moor in the canal

w: Rene Redzepi and Claus Meyer opened this foraging-obsessed kitchen in 2003, and it went on to be named World's Best Restaurant five times, credited with putting New Nordic cuisine on the map. It closed its dining room after a final Kyoto service, December 2024, now running as a food lab with pop-ups.
s: The kitchen that invented New Nordic cuisine
_facts: founded 2003 by Rene Redzepi and Claus Meyer
focus on foraging and New Nordic cuisine
named Best Restaurant in the World in 2010, 2011, 2012, 2014 and 2021
final regular dinner service in Kyoto, December 2024; now a food lab with pop-up residencies

w: Locals call it the Marble Church for its heavy rococo dome, the architectural anchor of the planned Frederiksstaden district. It stands due west of Amalienborg Palace, the Evangelical Lutheran centrepiece of one of Copenhagen's most orderly quarters.
_facts: popularly known as the Marble Church for its rococo architecture
focal point of the Frederiksstaden district
located due west of Amalienborg Palace

w: Named for Princess Charlotte Amalie, who built the original house, this summer palace was rebuilt for Crown Prince Frederick VIII in the 1880s -- then spent 1935 to 2017 as a fisheries research station, not a royal retreat. It's a concert venue now, its Great Hall occasionally filled with music instead of scientists.

_facts: former royal summer residence, named after Princess Charlotte Amalie

w: Denmark's only single-artist museum is devoted to sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen, who spent four decades carving Neoclassical marble in Rome before Copenhagen raised public funds to bring him -- and his life's work -- home. The purpose-built museum on Slotsholmen opened in 1848, four years after his death.
_facts: single-artist museum dedicated to sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen (1770-1844)

w: This is the sixth city hall to stand on the site, a National Romantic pile designed by Martin Nyrop and built between 1892 and 1905. It still houses the City Council chambers and the Lord Mayor's office, presiding over the square that shares its name.

_facts: sixth incarnation of Copenhagen City Hall

w: Built as a five-pointed star fort, this citadel is one of the best-preserved fortifications left in Northern Europe -- once part of a ring of ramparts around the whole city, of which only the Christianshavn stretch survives elsewhere. Inside the walls: a windmill, a church, and a public park shared with the military.
s: Star-shaped citadel, one of Europe's best-preserved

pentagon shape with bastions at its corners
